query: Why do some incidents take longer to resolve?

per_column.name: incident_category
per_column.rationale: The type/nature of the incident (connectivity, email, database) is a constitutive aspect of why delays arise -- it decomposes delay reasons by the domain of the problem.

per_column.name: incident_complexity
per_column.rationale: Complexity of the incident (system failure, escalation required, service degradation) is an intrinsic aspect of the delay-reason concept: harder incidents contribute a distinct facet of why resolution takes longer.

per_column.name: incident_scope
per_column.rationale: Scope/breadth of impact (individual vs system-wide vs departmental) is a genuine aspect of what makes an incident's resolution slow -- a constitutive facet of delay reasons.

per_column.name: assigned_technician
per_column.rationale: The identity of the technician is an external attribute correlated with resolution time, not an aspect OF the delay-reason concept itself. It is a predictor/actor, not a part of the reason.

per_column.name: same_technician_closure
per_column.rationale: Whether the same technician closed the incident is a process/handoff attribute correlated with delay, not a constitutive facet (an 'aspect of') the delay-reason concept.

judge.rationale: Three columns (category, complexity, scope) are genuine constitutive facets that decompose the delay-reason concept into aspects of the incident itself. However, complexity and scope partially overlap (e.g., 'system_wide' scope and 'system_failure' complexity capture related severity/breadth notions), lowering mutual exclusivity. The remaining two columns (assigned_technician, same_technician_closure) are external predictors/process attributes, not facets, so they do not satisfy the meronymy claim. The facet set covers problem-type, difficulty, and impact-breadth but omits process/lifecycle aspects of delay (queueing/wait time, dependency-on-third-party, information availability), so exhaustiveness is moderate.
